question.problem: Find the radius of curvature for the curve $r(t)=2{e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{2t}\,j$ at $t=0.$
question.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

The radius of curvature $R$ is defined as
$R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}.$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=2{e}^{t},\,y(t)={e}^{2t}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =2{e}^{t},\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =2{e}^{2t} \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =2{e}^{t},\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =4{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|2{e}^{t}\cdot 4{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{2t}\cdot 2{e}^{t}|}{{((2{e}^{t})^{2}+(2{e}^{2t})^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{3t}}{{(4{e}^{2t}+4{e}^{4t})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{(1+{e}^{2t})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{1}{2{(1+{e}^{2(0)})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{(1+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{1}{κ(0)}=4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
